extracted.intended_audience: researchers and students of scientific method, philosophers of science, and practicing scientists
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and choosing methods of scientific inquiry (deduction, experiment, observation) for investigating phenomena—especially complex phenomena arising from many concurrent causes—and the standards for establishing reliable laws and verifying theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: State laws as tendencies, not absolute results
rubrics_metrics.description: All laws of causation, in consequence of their liability to be counteracted, require to be stated in words affirmative of tendencies only, and not of actual results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use terminology that expresses a tendency (e.g. 'pressure' as tendency to motion in mechanics). This avoids the misleading popular impression that general scientific truths have exceptions; what appear as exceptions are usually other concurrent causes. Example: say 'heavy bodies tend to fall' rather than 'all heavy bodies fall.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat concurrent principles as separate laws, not exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are not a law and an exception to that law... There are two laws, each possibly acting in the whole hundred cases, and bringing about a common effect by their conjunct operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not categorize a concurrent or modifying cause as an 'exception' to a principle. Instead, recognize multiple principles acting jointly; explain apparent counterexamples as the influence of additional causes (example: atmospheric resistance vs gravitation for a balloon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose method based on composition of causes (method selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditions of a phenomenon which arises from a composition of causes, may be investigated either deductively or experimentally. The deductive (a priori) method is often the only feasible one for complex phenomena; the a posteriori (experimental/observational) methods are limited by plurality of causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When effects are the result of many concurrent causes (physiology, politics, history), favor the deductive method (derive complex-law from laws of separate causes). Use experimental/observational methods when causes can be isolated or their laws are accessible from simpler instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of simple observation (Method of Agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of simple observation (collating instances of the effect) is inapplicable to ascertain the conditions of effects dependent on many concurring causes; it yields at best a vague general impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on mere collation of instances to infer causation in multicausal contexts—abundant confounding causes will produce recoveries or failures irrespective of the candidate cause (example: mercury in disease). Use this method only where plurality of causes is minimal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental precautions: control circumstances and confounders
rubrics_metrics.description: When we devise an experiment to ascertain the effect of a given agent, there are certain precautions which we never, if we can help it, omit. In the first place, we introduce the agent into the midst of a set of circumstances which we have exactly ascertained... we require, also, that none of the circumstances which we do know shall have effects susceptible of being confounded with those of the agents whose properties we wish to study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure initial conditions are well ascertained; exclude or account for other causes that could be composed with the agent's effect. If other causes must be present, make them such that their influence can be computed and subtracted so the agent's residual effect is apparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical method must be purely empirical to test complex cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimental method does not derive the law of a complex case from the simpler laws which conspire to produce it, but makes its experiments directly upon the complex case... We must make entire abstraction of all knowledge of the simpler tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using an empirical test to determine whether an agent tends to produce a complex effect, design trials that address the complex case directly without relying on prior deductions about component mechanisms. Recognize, however, that in practice this ideal is often unattainable for multicausal phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental feasibility depends on effect size and dominance
rubrics_metrics.description: Some causes indeed there are which are more potent than any counteracting causes to which they are commonly exposed; and accordingly there are some truths in medicine which are sufficiently proved by direct experiment... they succeed in so large a proportion of cases, and against such powerful obstacles, that their tendency to restore health... may be regarded as an experimental truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct experiment can establish causal tendencies when the agent's effect is large and frequently realized despite other causes (specific remedies like quinine). For small or marginal causes, experiments on complex systems will often be inconclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive Method structure: induction, ratiocination, verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deductive Method consists of three operations: the first, one of direct induction; the second, of ratiocination; the third, of verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply deduction only after (1) obtaining laws of separate causes (by induction/experiment), (2) reasoning from those laws to compute effects of combinations (ratiocination), and (3) verifying deduced conclusions against observation or experiment where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain laws of separate causes as prerequisite to deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The first requisite... is to know the laws of those tendencies; the law of each of the concurrent causes: and this supposes a previous process of observation or experiment upon each cause separately; or else a previous deduction, which also must depend for its ultimate premises on observation or experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study each causal tendency in isolation if possible (or deduce it from simpler laws grounded in observation). Prefer instances where the tendency operates alone or with calculable agencies. Use methods like concomitant variations, pathological cases, or controlled experiments in simpler settings to obtain these laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pathological or artificial perturbations as experimental substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathological facts, or... diseases in their different forms and degrees, afford in the case of physiological investigation the most valuable equivalent to experimentation properly so called... we can produce pathological facts artificially: we can try experiments... by subjecting the living being to some external agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In physiology, exploit naturally occurring localized disturbances (pathology) or introduce controlled perturbations (nerve section, agents) to reveal functions. Prefer early stages of derangement when effects remain local. For general laws, perform experiments in stable (healthy) conditions when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratiocination limitations: mathematical and practical complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: When our knowledge of the causes is so perfect as to extend to the exact numerical laws which they observe... very often involves processes of calculation... In many complex cases the theorems of number and geometry are insufficient and calculation transcends mathematical power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that even with correct premises, computing the combined effect of many causes may be infeasible; approximate reasoning or qualitative deduction may be necessary. Do not overstate precision when calculations rest on incomplete numerical laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification as indispensable test of deductive conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: To warrant reliance on the general conclusions arrived at by deduction, these conclusions must be found, on careful comparison, to accord with the results of direct observation wherever it can be had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always compare deductive predictions with empirical experience where possible. If observed cases contradict deductions, either identify what frustrated the predicted effect or regard the theory as imperfect and unready for reliance.
